events.excerpt: Description A few small nit cleanups on the synchronizer component in consensus. Behavior change: fetch_blocks_from_peers now returns as soon as no request is in flight, instead of idling until the 4s FETCH_FROM_PEERS_TIMEOUT. This affects two cases: no request was sent because every selected block was already locked, or the last outstanding request failed with no peer left to retry on. In both cases no further network request is sent, and a failed request still waits the full 2s request timeout, so periodic runs cannot repeat faster than every ~2s on failures. The only new cost is local: while all selected blocks are locked, the scheduler polls get_missing_blocks at its default 200ms cadence instead of every 4s, which is the same cadence it already uses during fast successful sync. events.excerpt: Summary This proposal introduces post-quantum signature aggregation with leanVM in shadow mode . BLS remains the only authority for aggregates: consensus validity depends on BLS alone, exactly as today. leanVM aggregates and proofs are produced and verified alongside BLS, but their results have no effect on consensus. They are only measured, compared, and reported. When PQ/AI day arrives, an emergency hard fork simply retires BLS and enables leanVM in full. By “PQ/AI day” we mean the point at which quantum computers, or AI-assisted cryptanalysis, make BLS unsafe to rely on. Motivation Ethereum has to be ready for post-quantum signatures well before BLS is actually broken. Waiting until the last moment would mean deploying new, complex code to mainnet in a hurry. Giving leanVM authority early has its own risk: leanVM is new code that hasn’t been tested in production. However carefully it is built and audited, we can’t rule out a soundness bug that accepts an invalid proof, or a liveness bug that rejects a valid one. The main benefit of shadow mode is that Ethereum isn’t put at risk from a leanVM bug before PQ/AI day arrives. Because leanVM has no authority, a leanVM bug can’t break Ethereum’s security or halt the chain. At the same time, leanVM runs on mainnet under real load, so by the time it needs authority it is battle-tested code rather than something enabled in a hurry. events.excerpt: This is the fourth post in a series expanding on our governance stack. [Post 0: Overview] | Post 1: The Iris Oracle | Post 2: Multi-JAM Federation . Today: Layer 2 — decisions without parties. The infrastructure problem (Layer 0) and the identity problem (Layer 1) are hard engineering challenges. Every democratic system ever built has failed in at least one of the same ways: Token-weighted voting — the wealthy decide. One token, one vote is plutocracy by definition. events.excerpt: Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections. Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory. The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected. "This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time." You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems. Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected. And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load. "It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service." events.excerpt: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. events.excerpt: I would like to discuss a wallet design built around three components: Lindell 2-of-2 MPC signing, QR-only initialization, and encrypted NFC communication between a computer and a phone. The goal is to keep the convenience of a desktop wallet while ensuring that compromising either device alone does not provide unilateral signing authority. Lindell 2-of-2 MPC as the signing foundation The computer and phone each hold a private share of one joint signing key. Neither device holds the complete private key. Using a reviewed implementation of Lindell’s two-party ECDSA protocol , both devices interact to compute a signature without revealing their shares or reconstructing the complete private key. For Ethereum, the implementation would use secp256k1 and produce one ordinary ECDSA signature under the joint public key. The wallet can therefore use a normal Ethereum address without requiring an on-chain multisignature contract. The 2-of-2 requirement comes from the signing protocol itself: obtaining the computer’s share alone is insufficient, and obtaining the phone’s share alone is also insufficient. Both devices must participate in signing the same transaction. Initialize entirely through QR codes Initialization takes place before connecting the NFC reader. Each device generates its own secret contribution, and the two devices carry out the required key-generation exchanges through bidirectional QR codes. events.excerpt: Keeping sensitive data within national borders might satisfy a residency requirement. But does it mean your organization is genuinely in control? Not necessarily. events.excerpt: Every so often a flaw comes along that shows how fast the ground can shift under IT and security teams. PHP2Shell, a pair of critical flaws in PHP, was one of them. Details leaked before the planned disclosure, frontier AI helped researchers find the flaws, and PHP shipped fixes the next day. For many teams, though, the patch was the easy part. So what does it take to respond at that speed, and where should teams begin? What does governed autonomous IT look like in practice? Picture a loop. Software finds where a risk lives and ranks what matters most. It proposes a fix, then, inside limits people define, carries it out and checks that it worked. Routine, low-risk actions can run on their own. Higher-impact ones wait for a person to approve. A few are never handed over at all. Each step leaves a record that someone can review and reverse. What challenges do IT and security teams face today? Three problems keep coming up. The first is visibility. PHP2Shell reportedly sat undetected for more than a decade. For these two flaws, the fix was a version upgrade. The hard part was finding every copy of PHP, including copies bundled inside other software or extracted by hand onto Windows machines that never registered as installed applications. Then teams had to work out which copies the internet could reach and check for signs of earlier attack. An inventory built from a periodic snapshot can't answer those questions on the day they matter. The second is tool-hopping. events.excerpt: TL;DR A contract on Base checks every Zcash block header against Zcash’s consensus rules: the Equihash (200, 9) solution on the EIP-152 BLAKE2b precompile, the difficulty adjustment (including NU7’s 25-second blocks), the time rules and cumulative work. Contracts can then read Zcash’s best chain without trusting a bridge, a committee or whoever relays. Anyone can feed it; a feeder can delay the relay but cannot make it accept a header Zcash’s rules reject. One header costs about 626k gas (mean, whole transaction); Equihash is 361k of it. Following Zcash at 25-second blocks is ~3,456 headers, ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ gas a day: about 0.01 ETH a day at Base’s 0.005 gwei. A relay deployed with Mainnet parameters on 29 October 2026 crossed Zcash Mainnet’s NU7 activation (height 3,543,405, 6 November 2026) without a redeploy and followed the 5,405 headers after it. On top of the relay: a RISC Zero proof (Groth16-wrapped, 256,720 gas to verify on Base) that a shielded payment of at least an amount went to a receiver an app committed to, with a memo naming the app’s reference, inside the ZIP 221 chain history of a header the relay holds. The transaction id, the note, the block and the address never reach the EVM chain. A real Testnet payment was proven in 81 s on a rented RTX 4090, for about one cent. Testnets only, unaudited. events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface. Existing ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 contracts support it with no change, and a client that does not know the scheme sees a URI it can ignore. PR: Add ERC: Onchain URI Scheme by nxt3d · Pull Request #2158 · ethereum/ERCs · GitHub Feedback is welcome, especially from wallets, marketplaces, and indexers. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic

events.excerpt: Hi all, If you work with more than one Cosmos chain, you’ve probably hit this: chain binaries don’t update themselves. This is made possible by using AI models to load memory pages in and out of cheaper NVMe storage before your operating system or apps ever know they need it — kind of like SWAP or a Windows page file, but smarter. Everyone's favorite buzzword to the rescue Even in systems with high memory utilization, where (say) 95 percent of the memory is "in use," a lot of it isn't actively being used, he explained. He cited a Meta research paper that showed that between 50 and 80 percent of memory pages hadn't been touched in five minutes, ten minutes, or even longer. "Five minutes to Epyc is an eternity." Mext technology aims to offload those infrequently accessed pages to flash. The challenge, Smerdon explains, is that while flash may be 50x cheaper per bit, 30x lower power per bit, it's also 500x slower. events.excerpt: Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models. Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks. Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI. That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.” Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.” The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons. events.excerpt: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. The end of the bytecode is the other place it breaks. solc appends the IPFS hash of the metadata file, and the metadata holds a hash of every source file, so a changed comment changes the tail. I tried it on a small contract with one immutable: adding one comment line changed exactly the 32 bytes of that hash and nothing else. If everything matches except the tail, the compiled logic is the same but the sources are not the ones

events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX). The test takes 30 seconds and uses no API keys. The full methodology, results, and test script are at The Short Version — The Rogue Wave — sections 17 and 18. What needs to change: The per-asset threshold model must be replaced with a joint probability model that accounts for tail correlation acro

events.excerpt: ERC-3668 (CCIP-Read) lets a contract hand a read off to a gateway, but the gateway either has to be trusted or has to return a proof the contract can verify. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. The chain and address are encoded as an ERC-7930 Interoperable Address, for example USDC on Base. x-chain:0x0001000002210514833589fcd6edb6e08f4c7c32d4f71b54bda02913 An optional ?finalized=true makes the read at the finalized block instead of the latest one. The client alone decides whether it can safely read a given chain, and never takes RPC endpoints from the contract. Nested x-chain lookups are not followed, so each call makes at most one cross-chain hop. Contracts can also tell when a client does not support the ERC. They add a data: URL after the x-chain URL, which only older clients reach, and it delivers the single byte 0xff to the callback, a value no real ABI encoded result can have. The ERC changes no interfaces, it only adds a URL scheme to the existing urls list. PR: Add ERC: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read by nxt3d · Pull Request #2078 · ethereum/ERCs · GitHub Feedback is welcom
events.title: ERC-8446: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read

events.excerpt: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. events.excerpt: The following is an opinion post reflecting my vision for a possible design direction for Ethereum, not a concrete design. What I argue for is to rethink the notions of scaling, availability, and finality according to the principles of elasticity. TL;DR Ethereum’s capacity is configured in advance: one block per slot, a fixed slot time, a gas limit and a size limit. Price matches demand to it, and safety margins cover for the network. No protocol-wide rule adapts capacity limits to measured resource pressure. Elasticity is first of all about robustness. An elastic system measures what it can carry and takes on less when it is falling behind. A system without that feedback is the kind that goes into congestion collapse, and Ethereum’s overload incidents look like it. Scaling comes with it. A system that can back off can afford to run close to what the network and the nodes can carry, where a fixed margin has to pay for the worst day every day. TCP is the working example: its congestion control was built to stop collapses, and it is also much of why the same protocol, with small changes, runs on modems and on fibre. I look at the mempool and the unfinalized available chain as two grey areas of work in flight. The second one, its size and what it would cost to lose, is the control signal I think we are missing. events.excerpt: "Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work. Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors. One-shot inference XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang ), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google. "LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search. These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. events.excerpt: UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better. Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem. There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd , an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT . Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear. Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands. The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery. Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware."

events.excerpt: When a module limits what governance can do with it, a cap on what a treasury pays out per week or a list of addresses a reserve is allowed to pay, the easy place for that limit is the module’s params. The authority for MsgUpdateParams is then the same gov account the limit is meant to hold back. That came up in the Luggom thread here in October, and the fix was in their repo the same day. I think it’s general enough for its own topic, because it’s easy to miss when you read the module on its own. What x/gov does when a proposal passes In SDK v0.53.8, the version Gaia v29 runs, the gov EndBlocker tallies the vote and, if it passed, opens one cached context and runs the proposal’s messages in the order they were submitted ( abci.go L166-L217 ). Every message sees what the ones before it wrote. If one fails, nothing is written and the proposal is marked failed. So a proposal with a MsgUpdateParams that adds a payee or raises the cap, followed by the spend, passes the module’s check in the same block. Nothing runs before the vote either. At submission SubmitProposal runs each message’s ValidateBasic , checks that its only signer is the gov account and that the router knows the type ( proposal.go L46-L69 ), and that’s it. Voters do see both messages, if they open the proposal and read them. The summary is free text. Two proposals don’t fix it Splitting it into a params proposal and a spend proposal looks safer, but both can be in voting at the same time. If the params one ends first, the spend passes when it executes. Voters get two votes on the same thing and that’s all. x/gov

Specification Draft PR #2159 Problem and scope A payment institution needs to distinguish a customer’s business entries from changes to the spending capacity it grants. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. This proposal defines a common contract interface for those records and controls. It can serve an institution’s own business independently or compose with an on-chain payment protocol. It does not issue or transfer assets, establish customer identity, or prove that funds have been frozen or settled. Account model and interface Each account is scoped by (account, institution) . An institution can serve payer accounts, merchant accounts, or both; the same address at two institutions does not share records or capacity. Holding the account’s private key does not grant permission to write entries. events.excerpt: The prdoc for the XCMv3 removal ( pr_13629.prdoc ) has a line the announcement here doesn’t have: “Assets trapped under a v3 hash become unclaimable.” I wanted to know how much that is on Polkadot, so I pulled every AssetsTrapped event for the relay and Asset Hub from Statescan and checked each hash against AssetTraps storage today. On the relay, 299 trap entries from the v3 period are still unclaimed, with 673.7 DOT in them. On Asset Hub there are 177, with 263.2 DOT and a bit of USDT and USDC. On both chains the v3 period runs from June 2023 to April 2024, when the runtimes moved to v4. Most of it belongs to ordinary accounts, not parachains. That’s 636.9 DOT across 224 accounts on the relay and 262.6 DOT across 116 accounts on Asset Hub. How it got there All but one of those account traps came from limitedTeleportAssets between the relay and Asset Hub. On the relay, most of the ones I opened show KilledAccount , then AssetsTrapped , then Attempted failing with FailedToTransactAsset . The account sent its whole balance, got reaped in the same transaction, and what the program had withdrawn went into the trap. On Asset Hub they fail with the same error, but the accounts weren’t reaped and most still hold DOT. A wallet team asked about these here in May 2024, and the answer then was claim_assets with the exact assets from the event. Why the removal ends it pallet-xcm stores a trap as a count under blake2_256(origin, VersionedAssets) , so the version is part of the key. claim_assets reads the version from the assets you pass and makes it the ticket, GeneralIndex(3) for these

The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. events.excerpt: TL;DR On an 8 GB M2 running leanVM at commit df7d122, hash-based accumulation did not beat leanVM’s full-verifier recursion inside an aggregator. Our best batching design also missed its 15% gate once the leaf size was tuned. Negative results (D1, D2, D3-S). Folding the whole leanVM step relation runs at 260 ns per witness element, against leanVM’s 55 ns per committed word (Verified rates). Accumulating children’s openings across merges spends about 57k cycles per step to save at most 46k (Verified counts). Cost anatomy (Verified). Verifying one child inside a merge costs 186.8k VM cycles. Its WHIR opening is 55% of that. Merkle hashing is 12% of the cycles but 79% of the Keccak calls. 73% of the JUMP rows are subfield checks. Batched child openings (B’-L1). One shared WHIR opening from level 1 saves 32.8k cycles per child (17.6%, Verified by cost emulation). A round-by-round sketch keeps leanVM’s bounds (Inferred). For 1,500 signatures it is still 2.4% slower at the slot deadline than the baseline at the baseline’s best configuration. Configuration rule (Verified on this machine). A merge node that steps from mu 25 to mu 26 takes 1.4 to 1.8x longer for about 3% more committed words. Aggregating 1,500 signatures as 5 leaves of 300 instead of 6 of 250 keeps the node at mu 25. events.excerpt: TL;DR: An opt-in, public, per-account “protected” flag for ERC-20s. Small sends stay instant; anything bigger is scheduled and can be cancelled by a pre-registered backup wallet; a “stress” action sweeps everything to the backup and locks it, which also helps against wrench attacks. Turning protection on is instant; weakening it (off, higher limit, shorter waits, new backup) takes a delay the holder picks. Why: Today a stolen key or a coerced holder means an instant, final drain. Existing approaches are per-transfer (SLOW), need recipient cooperation (ERC-8236), need judges (ERC-20R), protect protocols rather than users (ERC-7265), or only work in one smart wallet. This puts the protection in the token, so it works for any holder and any wallet, including plain EOAs. How it works: protect(backup, dailyLimit, holdWindow, offDelay, lockDuration, fastLane) : instant. Over-limit transferFrom reverts (never returns true without moving tokens, so routers, vaults and lenders can’t be fooled). Over-limit transfer from an EOA may be auto-scheduled, so wallet “Send” buttons just work. queueTransfer → hold window → anyone can executeTransfer ; the owner or backup can cancelTransfer ; with the opt-in fast lane, the backup can approveTransfer to skip the wait. stress(account) : cancels everything pending and moves the balance to the backup, locked for a preconfigured duration (the caller can’t choose it, so a coerced caller can’t pick zero). Receiving is always instant; unprotected accounts are plain ERC-20. Status: We built a working reference implementation at ETHGlobal Mumbai: a 1:1

events.excerpt: How large can EIP-8141’s validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark Authors: Stefano De Angelis , Daniil Ankushin , Manuel Arto . All at Nethermind. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . TL;DR EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100k; too low for a Groth16 privacy transfer or post-quantum signatures . Raising the cap is a DoS risk, since validation and block processing share the node’s CPU. An attacker can send transactions that use the whole cap and then fail, taking CPU from block processing for free. We tested this risk on a Nethermind node, flooding it with such transactions at caps from 100k to 500k, on one CPU core (the worst case) and three machines. Without in-client protections, block processing on our slowest machine stays within a 25 ms delay budget only up to 15M gas/s. With Nethermind allowing up to about 100 failing tx/s per connection, that limits the cap to the current 100k. On frame transactions a shielded pool pays its own gas, so a private withdrawal needs no relayer. We ran a real BN254 Groth16 pool this way on current Nethermind master: a withdrawal costs 679,322 gas. With EIP-8250 nonce keys, many withdrawals can come from the one pool address at once. Two things do not work yet. The proof check is over the spec cap on validation gas, and a pool cannot pay for a call from the user’s own address. The pool we ran is soispoke’s minimal-shielded-pool ( GitHub - soispoke/minimal-shielded-pool · GitHub ). How a withdrawal works In a withdrawal the pool is the sender. Its VERIFY code checks the zk proof and approves execution and payment. The user needs no funded account and does not appear in the transaction. Two drafts make this safe in a public mempool. With EIP-8250 the pool uses the note’s nullifiers as nonce keys. Each withdrawal has its own nonce key, so withdrawals with the pool as sender do not compete for one nonce. A side effect: a nullifier that was already used is a used nonce key, so the protocol refuses a double spend before the pool’s code runs. With EIP-8272 the transaction checks the pool’s Merkle root against a contract of recent roots before the pool’s code runs, so a mempool node never reads the pool’s storage. events.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison.
